articles.title: The last time a Kansas Democrat was in the Senate, the Wizard of Oz was in cinemas
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton, a pastor, has made history as the first Kansas Democrat to win the Senate in almost 100 years.
articles.body:
Kansas woke up on Wednesday to sunny skies and historic new leadership after days of rain, hail and tornado warnings - amid a tempestuous election battle that ultimately swept a new brand of blue politics into the deep-red state.

Democrat and church pastor Adam Hamilton claimed victory Tuesday night over Republican incumbent and staunch Trump supporter Senator Roger Marshall, marking the first time a Democrat won the seat since 1932.

The 62-year-old leader of the US's largest United Methodist congregation - with 24,000 congregants - had promised voters civility, moderate policy stances and and open ear to their concerns. He'd invoked the state's most famous cultural touchstone, the Wizard of Oz, on the campaign trail, telling Kansans: "What we need in Washington right now is we need senators with a brain who use it, with a heart who feel with it, and who have courage and speak up because of it."

When the race was called in Hamilton's favour, voters all over Kansas - from lifelong Republicans in tiny unincorporated communities to dyed-in-the-wool liberals who'd felt disenfranchised for decades - erupted in cheers and sighs of relief.

In Wichita, a manufacturing city in the heart of the state, around 100 attendees celebrated as TV pundits onscreen spoke of a "blue tsunami" - cheering as Democrats swept not just Kansas seats but also races across the nation.

"I have lived in Kansas for 30-something years, and I have felt all of those years like I voted and my vote was never counted," said Laura Elliott, 71, sitting at a high-top table with three others.

"We did it!" shouted Chuck Schmidt, 76, hugging a younger voter as he credited upcoming generations with the party's success.

"People are fed up with the chaos and the corruption," Schmidt, a former state representative, told BBC. "People in Kansas, for some reason, have gotten conditioned to just vote for the R - and they haven't realised there was another alternative."

Faith has long been a deciding factor for many Kansas voters. A 2025 report from the Pew Research Center ranked the state as the 10th most religious in the US, with 70% of Kansans identifying as Christian and nearly 30% as evangelical Protestants - a group that has overwhelmingly backed Trump and the Republican Party in recent years.

In Great Bend, Marshall's hometown, Navy veteran Richard Elmore listed abortion, transgender issues, illegal immigration and "the gay rights issue" as some of the reasons he backed the Republican candidate.

"Anybody that'd say they were a Christian and not honour those things are lying to themselves and others," said the 77-year-old grandfather, who believes an angel is protecting Trump, otherwise "he'd be dead".

The Marshall campaign had painted Hamilton as a radical liberal whose views contradicted Biblical teachings – but the strategy failed to curb the Democrat's momentum.

In Marshall's concession speech, the outgoing senator quoted scripture – and called the loss "humbling".

"I don't have any answers," he said. "I'll just tell you it's been the greatest honour of my life to serve the state of Kansas for ten years."

As the founding pastor of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection, Hamilton told voters his faith is what inspires his belief that the government should help care for the poor and vulnerable.

But some took issue with his positions; Richard Friedeman, a lawyer and Republican Party chair of Kansas' Barton County, accused the pastor of being "very, very liberal - and he has the ability that liberal pastors have of telling you one thing and turning right around and telling somebody else the opposite".

Friedeman was cautiously optimistic on election day as he discussed the race from his Great Bend home, saying he believed Marshall, a personal friend and "good Republican voter," had "done a good job" during his time in office.

But he conceded that the Republican party was embattled.

"I think there's going to be a reckoning for the way Trump has alienated so many people... I think it's going to be hard for awhile," he said.

His prediction proved true, as voters in Republican strongholds like Iowa, South Carolina and Texas turned out for Democratic candidates.

Even in Mississippi, the heart of America's bible belt, the race was neck and neck at the time of publication - a feat once thought nearly impossible for the Democratic Party.

Most pundits and pollsters are viewing these historic victories as rebukes of Trump's second-term agenda, such as aggressive immigration policies, a war in Iran and global tariffs that have contributed to the rising cost of living.

The day before the election, on a rainy afternoon filled with squalls and hail, dozens of Hamilton supporters turned out for a last-minute canvas in the university town of Lawrence, Kansas. Among them were retired teacher Sharron Witters, 77, and her husband Lynn, 78, a former forestry professor and pastor of 25 years.

As evangelical Christians, they said Hamilton's candidacy motivated them to put out signs on their lawn and knock on doors for the first time. They set out with maps and lists, as Sharron navigated their silver VW SUV from address to address in a well-heeled Lawrence neighbourhood.

Hamilton, Sharron said, "doesn't sound like a politician".

"What a delight to stand and listen to somebody whose sentences make sense," she said.

"Wouldn't it be wonderful if he actually motivated people to work across the aisle?

She noted how other evangelical Christians had backed Trump "because he said, 'I'm against abortion'".

But she and her husband, "felt, from the very beginning, that [Trump] was a wolf in sheep's clothing".

Hamilton's campaign galvanised a powerful cross-section of Kansas society - from Republicans voting blue for the first time to long-time liberals initially skeptical of his more moderate positions.

In Great Bend, a town of 14,000 bordered by farmland and myriad anti-abortion billboards along country roads, lifelong Republican Dan Bonine, 85, cast his first vote for a Democrat.

The retired banker had been one of Marshall's earliest supporters when the physician began his political career - but was swayed by Hamilton's presence and positions.

"Ronald Reagan was really a great leader to bring us together, and I think Adam Hamilton possesses much of that same kind of leadership skill," Bonine told the BBC, adding that "in my lifetime we've only had three or four" politicians of such calibre.

"He's just an awesome, awesome leader, and his values are rock solid."

In Kansas, voters say they were inspired not just by their frustration with Trump and his policies but also, like Bonine, by Hamilton's charisma and positions - particularly in contrast with Marshall's performance over the last six years.

Critics argued that the Republican senator prioritised Trump loyalty over the needs of Kansas, with much attention paid to Marshall's residence in Florida - where many voters felt he spent more of his time and attention than in his home state.

Registered Republican Bryan Drescher, 40, grew up in Great Bend - and Marshall coached him in baseball. He voted for the senator six years ago but noted that Marshall had a reputation for being "brash" and "quick to judge" - citing, for example, a 2025 town hall that the Senator abruptly ended when challenged.

"I want someone… who's going to bring us back to the middle and back to the table," Drescher said. Hamilton, he felt, fit that description.

The air was thick with celebration and relief as Wichita attendees left the party before midnight on Tuesday, heading home to digest Hamilton's win and what it meant for Kansas' future.

Retired teacher Judith Ney, 74, sat at the party with her fellow education retiree, Sheryl Loveland. The pair were initially nervous wrecks, they said, hoping desperately that Hamilton and other Democrats would prevail.

Now they were "so stinking happy," Loveland said.

"I've been waiting for decades for this kind of a night," said Chuck Schmidt, the former Democratic state rep, beaming widely under his University of Kansas baseball cap. "And we're finally getting, I think, what we've been trying to get to."

articles.title: County Louth: Robert O'Connor found guilty of manslaughter for killing 3 family members
articles.summary: Louise O'Connor, Mark O'Connor, and Evan O'Connor were found dead at their rural home in Drumgowna in 2025.
articles.body:
A 32-year-old man who killed his parents and younger brother has been found not guilty of their murders but guilty of manslaughter by diminished responsibility.

The jury at the Central Criminal Court in Dublin accepted evidence given by two psychiatrists that Robert O'Connor was suffering from a relapse of schizophrenia when he stabbed the three members of his family to death in September 2025.

Louise O'Connor, 56, her 54-year-old husband Mark O'Connor, and their son Evan, 27, were found dead at their home in Drumgowna, County Louth.

Lawyers for Robert O'Connor had asked jurors to consider finding him not guilty by reason of insanity so that he could get the "proper mental health treatment".

Robert O'Connor, of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk, had pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility to the triple murder between 28 and 29 September, 2025.

The jury was told that the defendant accepted he caused the death of the three victims, who had sustained a combined 139 stab wounds.

In his closing speech, the defendant's lawyer, Michael Bowman SC, told the court that O'Connor was previously misdiagnosed and, it seemed, on subsequent occasions his illness was put down to the consumption of drugs.

The special verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity, the barrister told the trial jury, carried with it the hope and expectation that the defendant would be "properly treated in an appropriate environment for the first time in his life".

Whilst both expert psychiatric witnesses were of the view that guilty of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility would be appropriate verdicts, they differed on whether the defendant qualified for the special verdicts of not guilty by reason of insanity.

Consultant forensic psychiatrist Dr Fiona Toal, called to give evidence by the defence, testified that O'Connor did not know what he was doing was wrong and could not refrain from committing the act.

She found that O'Connor met the criteria for special verdicts of not guilty by reason of insanity.

Psychiatrist Dr Ronan Mullaney, for the prosecution, had told the trial that O'Connor met the criteria for verdicts of guilty of manslaughter by diminished responsibility and did not meet the criteria for the special verdicts of not guilty by reason of insanity.

Dr Mullaney found the defendant had expressed remorse and his question to gardaí (Irish police) about "what kind of time" he might expect indicated "a good understanding of his role".

O'Connor had told gardaí he stabbed his brother Evan, who had autism, and later described in his interviews how his mother had asked him to let his younger brother go as he held them by knife point in their sitting room.

A pathologist testified that the majority of Evan's wounds were inflicted by his eldest brother while he was still alive.

O'Connor, who was not maintaining his schizophrenia medication and using cocaine in the months before the three killings, also told officers that he had a row with his parents over drugs, lost his head and only meant to kill his father and brother, but not his mother.

The jury of six men and six women spent four hours and eight minutes deliberating over two days before bringing in unanimous verdicts on each of the three counts.

After they had delivered their three verdicts, Mr Justice Mícheál P O'Higgins told the jury that it had been "a difficult and really very sad case".

O'Connor was remanded in custody until 14 December, when his sentence hearing will take place.

articles.title: Cocaine overtakes heroin as leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales
articles.summary: The number of deaths linked to cocaine use in England and Wales has nearly quadrupled in a decade.
articles.body:
The number of deaths from cocaine use in England and Wales has nearly quadrupled in a decade, overtaking those attributed to heroin for the first time.

Cocaine was linked to more than one in five drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025, more than any other single substance, with charities blaming its increased purity and availability.

Meanwhile a record 115 ketamine-linked deaths were registered, almost twice as many as in 2024, according to Office for National Statistics data .

The overall rate of drug deaths fell for the first time since 2012. But experts pointed out regional inequality was growing, with the rate of such deaths more than twice as high in the North East as in London.

There were 5,519 drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025 in England and Wales, the equivalent of 92.4 deaths per million people.

Of these, cocaine was mentioned in 1,233 cases - slightly fewer than the previous year but higher than the 1,210 deaths linked to heroin or morphine, which also marked a fall from the previous year's level.

However, deaths linked to opiate and opioid drugs combined were still higher. The ONS also said there was a lag between deaths occurring and being registered.

The fatality rate fell from 93.9 deaths per million people a year earlier, representing the first annual decline since 2012.

In September, National Records of Scotland said drug deaths there had risen by 11% in 2025 on the year before, marking the worst mortality rate in Europe

In May the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency said drug-related deaths rose by 7.1% between 2021-23 and 2022-24 .

Dr James Morgan, who specialises in addiction and mental health at London Metropolitan University, said while there had been a slight decrease in deaths "the numbers remain objectively high", with total drug fatalities in England and Wales roughly doubling since 2012.

"What we are seeing is increasing polarisation and growing inequalities, where the poorest regions are falling behind, and more affluent regions doing better," he said.

The steepest increases were found in formerly industrial areas with high levels of poverty and unemployment dating back to the 1980s, including the North East, Wales, Yorkshire and the Humber, the North West and the East Midlands.

Morgan pointed out that cocaine death figures included not only those who snorted the drug but also users who injected it or smoke crack cocaine in combination with opioids or counterfeit pharmaceutical drugs.

"The small decline in deaths related to cocaine should not be over-interpreted. Most important is that deaths relating to cocaine remain roughly quadruple what they were in 2015 and are now more frequent than deaths relating to heroin or morphine," he said.

Meanwhile, ketamine was referenced in 115 deaths last year - almost double the year before and up from just seven fatalities 10 years earlier.

Morgan said this was down to lower prices and use of the drug becoming normalised. He said there were increasing reports of young people becoming dependent on ketamine and suffering acute health difficulties such as bladder damage.

Mike Trace, CEO of the addiction charity Forward Trust, said drug poisoning deaths remained high because of factors including the proliferation of very strong synthetic opioid drugs called nitazenes .

"We know that increasingly potent drugs like nitazenes are making their way on to the market. We know that established drugs like cocaine are growing in purity which means they come with much higher risks to users," he said.

Nitazenes can be many times more potent than heroin and have been linked to hundreds of UK deaths.

Tom Powell and Nyk Irvin's brother Anthony Irvin died from drug poisoning in Ramsgate in September 2025 at the age of 52.

His siblings believe his death was caused by a supply of drugs being contaminated with synthetic opioids, but say delays in blood testing mean they will never know for sure.

"Today's figures are shocking," Powell said. "We are fighting to wake people up to the scale of the problem."

articles.body:
U.S. President Trump says U.S. had begun "major combat operations" in Iran

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the Iran war has been ‌worth it despite acknowledging its role in ‌losses in US midterm elections in which his Republican party ​lost control of Congress.

"The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," he told reporters.

The Iran war was responsible for a ‌spike in gasoline ⁠prices that were seen as a strong factor in why Democrats made big ⁠gains in the elections.

Trump said the war has been worth it to stop Tehran from "having a ​nuclear weapon."

He ​said he was okay ​with Vice President JD ‌Vance's social media post earlier on Wednesday in which Vance referred to deep electoral losses and said "the reason we lost is the war."

"I can tell you that as far as that war ‌is concerned, I would have ​done nothing different," Trump said.

Trump ​also again said ​that if he had been on ‌the ballot, he believed "we would ​have won."

"But ​they just, you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it ​was incredible ‌and we weren't able to transfer the love ​to candidates," he said.

articles.summary: Two men pleaded guilty to using a defunct youth softball charity to secure concession work at two major stadiums and receiving more than $3.5 million in
articles.body: Two men pleaded guilty to using a defunct youth softball charity to secure concession work at two major stadiums and receiving more than $3.5 million in payments meant for charitable purposes. Noly Hermoso Ilarde and Martin Jose Rebollo Jr. posed as representatives of Chula Vista Fast Pitch, a defunct charity that provided support for youth softball activities. They applied and were selected to provide unpaid volunteer services at Petco Park and Snapdragon Stadium, with about 10% of concession sales going to the charity. The scheme brought in approximately $3.5 million from Delaware North and more than $250,000 from Aztec Shops.According to the US Department of Justice, the men paid each supposed volunteer about $50 per event and divided the remaining money between themselves. Neither man gave any money to the charity, and none of the funds went towards youth softball or other charitable activities.How the two men used a defunct charity to secure stadium concession workIlarde pleaded guilty in federal court on March 11, 2026, to wire fraud conspiracy. He admitted that he and Rebollo had presented themselves as Chula Vista Fast Pitch, a defunct charity that provided support for youth softball activities. The pair applied to provide volunteers for concession work at Petco Park and Snapdragon Stadium.Their arrangement involved supplying unpaid volunteers in exchange for approximately 10% of concession sales going to the charity. Instead, the men paid each supposed volunteer about $50 in cash for each event. They then divided the remaining money between themselves. The plea agreements stated that no funds were paid to the charity or used for any charitable purpose.More than $3.5 million diverted from stadium concession paymentsThe charity received approximately $3.5 million in payments from Delaware North, the hospitality management company responsible for concessions at Petco Park. It also received more than $250,000 from Aztec Shops, the non-profit organisation in charge of concessions at Snapdragon Stadium. The two companies deposited the money into bank accounts controlled by Rebollo.Ilarde and Rebollo paid volunteers about $50 per event in cash and split the remaining money between themselves. Ilarde admitted that he personally gained more than $550,000 through the scheme. The payments from the stadium concession operations amounted to more than $3.5 million, based on the figures detailed in Ilarde’s plea agreement.What penalties do Ilarde and Rebollo face for the charity fraudRebollo pleaded guilty in December 2025 to wire fraud conspiracy, filing a false tax return, and Social Security fraud connected with the scheme. His plea agreement stated that his gain from the conspiracy exceeded $1.5 million.As reported by the US Department of Justice, Rebollo was scheduled to be sentenced on June 5, 2026. Ilarde, 57, from San Diego, pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy charges. Ilarde faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison and a fine of $250,000, or twice the gross gain or loss, whichever amount is greater.What did the federal investigation revealedThe case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, IRS Criminal Investigation and the Social Security Administration’s Office of the Inspector General. Ilarde’s plea agreement identified Delaware North and Aztec Shops as the organisations that made payments to accounts controlled by Rebollo.According to the US Department of Justice, the defendants did not pay any funds to Chula Vista Fast Pitch. It also stated that none of the money was used for youth softball activities or any other charitable or non-profit purpose. Rebollo’s guilty plea covered three offences that are wire fraud conspiracy, filing a false tax return, and failure to disclose an event to the Social Security Administration.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information. "We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too," Bukele wrote in a message on X directed at Haiti's criminal groups. Haiti’s National Police announced Tuesday, more than two weeks after the attack, that it had found the charred remains of the vehicle in the Santo neighborhood of Croix-des-Bouquets. Police said, however, they found no sign of the missing men. El Salvador says the men were abducted, the Haitian government says the soldiers are missing, and one gang leader says they are dead. In a post on X Tuesday, directed at the "Haitian people" and written in Haitian creole, Bukele recalled the 1806 assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who proclaimed Haiti’s independence from France in 1804 and who many regard as the founder of Haiti. "Dessalines liberated Haiti, but some people who were by his side betrayed him and killed him," Bukele said. "Those traitors still exist in Haiti." SUSPECTS IN HAITIAN PRESIDENT'S ASSASSINATION TRANSFERRED TO MIAMI, ACCUSED OF FUNDING PLOT WITH COVID FRAUD Bukele also reposted video of a helicopter engagement in Croix-des-Bouquets. "Gangs were attacking GSF soldiers from Chad," he wrote. "We arrived quickly and repelled the attackers with our attack helicopters." Unlike previous foreign interventions, Bukele's deployment has the backing of Haiti's transitional government. "The international force is not here to replace the state," Haitian Prime Minister Didier Fils-Aimé said Tuesday in his first remarks about the deployment. "They're here to support us." The question now is whether that model can be exported to Haiti, where gangs control large portions of Port-au-Prince and wield influence over key transportation routes and neighborhoods. articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: The first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate in American history wasted little time in igniting MAGA outrage, barely waiting for the confetti to settle before reminding President Trump and his veep JD Vance that they would have to get used to him.Abdul El-Sayed, the 42-year-old Michigan Democrat who defeated Republican Mike Rogers to make history, had a particularly choice message for Vance, who had spent the campaign attacking him. "JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January," he told cheering supporters at his victory celebration, casually using initials for the vice-president and throwing in a snarky endearment – “habibi” in Arabic is “my love”For Trump, who had repeatedly struggled with El-Sayed's name -- at one point derisively calling him "Mohammed" -- the incoming senator had an equally economical suggestion. "Donald, look, I know you struggle with my name. So after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator."It was an appropriately cheeky ending to a campaign in which Republicans had made El-Sayed’s Muslim faith a political issue, questioning his loyalties to America and associating him with radical Islamist groups without substantiating the allegations. Trump had gone so far as to suggest he is a security risk who wouldnot be allowed to enter the Senate without going through a metal detector.El-Sayed, however, is about as American as they come. Born and raised in Rochester Hills, Michigan, to Egyptian immigrant parents, he grew up in the Detroit suburbs, captained his high-school football, wrestling and lacrosse teams, graduated from the University of Michigan, became a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford and earned his medical degree at Columbia University. His wife, Sarah Jukaku, is also American-born, to Indian immigrant parents with roots in Karnataka's Bhatkal. A psychiatrist by profession, she and her family have given the Egyptian-American senator-elect a distinctly desi connection: El-Sayed has joked that after two decades of marriage, he might be more Indian than Arab.The Michigan victory was part of a wider advance by Muslim Americans in Congress at a time of rampant Islamophobia promoted by MAGA hardliners. Representatives Ilhan Omar of Minnesota and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, both frequent targets of Trump's political invective, comfortably secured fresh terms, while Aisha Wahab, the Afghan-American Democrat who entered Congress following a special election in August, also won a full term representing California.But the story of Tuesday's election was considerably bigger than Muslim representation; it was also a vindication of the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, which has spent years being told by its more cautious establishment colleagues that its politics might be popular on college campuses and social media but would struggle in the real world. The results have rather inconveniently challenged that assumption.Chennai-born Pramila Jayapal, the Indian-American former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, won another term in Washington state, ensuring that the party's left flank retains one of its most experienced and articulate voices. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, perhaps the most recognisable face of the progressive insurgency, also romped to re-election. They will be joined by a new crop of left-leaning lawmakers, including Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both from New York, and both backed by NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani. And just in case anyone thought socialism in America was dead, joining them in what will be at least a five-member cohort of Democratic socialists are Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, Donovan McKinney of Michigan, and Melat Kiros of Colorado.For the Democratic establishment, which has periodically tried to contain its insurgent wing, the results present an intriguing challenge. Capturing both the House and Senate will give Dems control of congressional committees, subpoena powers, the ability to investigate the administration, and make and break legislation. The progressive contingent will want to go further, pushing for a tougher stance on Israel, universal healthcare, higher taxes on the wealthy, stronger social protections and a more aggressive challenge to corporate power.It’s going to be a wild time in American politics…habibi.You use AI every day. articles.title: Srinagar MP’s exit part of BJP’s ‘Op Lotus’ plan in J&K, says  NC
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Governing National Conference (NC) in Jammu & Kashmir Wednesday described the resignation of its Srinagar MP, Aga Ruhullah Mehdi, as the
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Governing National Conference (NC) in Jammu & Kashmir Wednesday described the resignation of its Srinagar MP, Aga Ruhullah Mehdi, as the handiwork of BJP, saying the party had succeeded in its mission under ‘Operation Lotus’.Addressing a news conference at the party headquarters in Srinagar, NC legislators Salam Sagar and Sajad Shaheen said the MP’s departure was the outcome of a “planned and calculated” strategy.“BJP has succeeded in getting Aga Sahib (Mehdi) out of NC. He has now joined a force that has tried two or three times over the past 80-90 years to weaken us, but we managed to defeat those attempts earlier,” Sagar said.“What you witnessed yesterday (Tuesday) in Kashmir is similar to ‘Operation Lotus’ carried out in Parliament to engineer defections and get MPs to leave their parties. With Aga Sahib’s help, BJP’s agenda has been fulfilled,” the NC MLAs alleged.The duo termed Mehdi’s allegation that NC had abandoned its fight for restoration of J&K’s special status an excuse and ruse. “He (Mehdi) was with the party for 24 years. If he failed to realise in all these years that we are not sincere in following our agenda, as he has alleged, then it speaks about him, rather than the party,” Sagar said, adding: “We will never compromise on Articles 370 and 35A or the rights of the people of Jammu & Kashmir.”J&K deputy chief minister Surinder Choudhary accused BJP of misleading the NC MP, referring to its national vice-president Ram Madhav’s reported remark in Jammu on Tuesday that Mehdi held a rally in Budgam after his resignation with the blessings of “our people”.“Aga Sahib was a good and respectable person. BJP misled him, and Ram Madhav himself said yesterday said that Aga Sahib was their man,” Choudhary told media persons in Jammu on Wednesday.Responding to the allegations, BJP spokesperson Sajjad Yousuf Shah said the party had nothing to do with NC’s internal affairs. ‘Operation Lotus’ was a figment of NC’s imagination, he said, insisting that Ram Madhav was in Jammu under a preplanned party programme and his visit had nothing to do with the crisis in the governing party.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Scottish MPs call for law that allowed Indian national Manivannan to be elected to parliament to be overturned
articles.summary: LONDON: A Holyrood committee comprising members of Scotland’s parliament has recommended the Scottish govt reconsider its controversial policy of allowing
articles.body: LONDON: A Holyrood committee comprising members of Scotland’s parliament has recommended the Scottish govt reconsider its controversial policy of allowing foreign nationals with “limited leave to remain” to stand in Scottish parliament and local govt elections.The recommendation comes after Indian national Q Manivannan, from Chennai, was elected as an MSP to the Edinburgh and Lothians East seat in May for the Scottish Green Party, despite being on a student visa. His election triggered a political and public storm.The Scottish parliament’s Standards, Procedures and Public Appointments Committee, in a report, has now stated that it does not “accept the premise that there should be a general right for non-UK citizens with limited leave to remain to be councillors or MSPs”. It said that in the aftermath of the 2026 Scottish parliament elections, “some of the public were surprised to discover that these rules existed”.However, asked whether he would review the legislation, Scotland first minister John Swinney said: “We don’t intend to do so, no.” A spokesman for the Scottish Greens said: “There are thousands of people with limited leave to remain who live and work in Scotland. They should be able to stand for our parliament and councils.”The committee said the act appeared to “have run ahead of public opinion”, noting that a public consultation found that 77% of respondents disagreed with extending candidacy rights to foreigners with limited leave to remain (people on time-limited visas such as student visas).It was the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025 which extended candidacy rights to all foreign citizens with limited leave to remain in the UK.Prof Alistair Clark, at Newcastle University, gave evidence to the committee saying he could not find any international example of any other country offering this.The committee also noted “there could be an opportunity for candidates to be influenced by overseas actors” and this act created a risk of “foreign interference in the Scottish electoral process”.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New Jersey woman warned authorities about an oak tree on an adjoining utility-owned property; it later fell onto her home, and an appeals court upheld a jury's $173,000 damages award
articles.summary: A New Jersey homeowner who repeatedly warned officials about a dangerous oak tree on neighboring utility-owned land has won a major legal victory after
articles.body: A New Jersey homeowner who repeatedly warned officials about a dangerous oak tree on neighboring utility-owned land has won a major legal victory after the dying tree eventually fell onto her house. The Superior Court of New Jersey, Appellate Division, upheld a jury decision awarding the homeowner $173,000 in property damages. The ruling, recorded under docket number A-2181-23, rejected the utility property owner's attempt to overturn the jury's decision that it was responsible for the damage. The appeals court made clear that property owners cannot ignore warnings about dangerous conditions on their land. This is especially important when dying or unstable trees could fall and damage nearby homes.Repeated warnings preceded structural damageAccording to official court records from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Appellate Division, the dispute began when the homeowner noticed a large, damaged oak tree growing near the boundary of a neighboring property owned by a utility company. Worried that the tree could cause serious damage to her home, the woman made several attempts to warn the utility company and local officials about its rotting condition. She raised her concerns through both written messages and direct conversations over an extended period. Despite these warnings, the property owner failed to carry out the needed maintenance, check whether the tree was structurally safe, or remove its dangerous branches. The situation eventually became serious when the dying oak tree was uprooted and fell directly onto the homeowner's house. The impact caused major damage to the roof, the building's frame, and the inside of the home. The homeowner faced high repair costs and was also forced to leave the property temporarily.Trial court jury finds utility negligentAfter the incident, the homeowner filed a civil lawsuit over the property damage in the Law Division of the New Jersey Superior Court. She accused the utility company of negligence under common law and private nuisance. Her complaint argued that the company had a legal duty to keep its property reasonably safe and deal with known dangers that could predictably damage neighboring homes. During the trial, the homeowner presented records of her earlier communications with the utility company. These documents showed that the company had been informed about the tree's dangerous condition well before it fell. Experts in tree care and property valuation also gave evidence about the tree's visible decay and the full extent of the damage to the house. The jury ruled in favor of the homeowner. It found that the utility company had acted carelessly by failing to deal with a known danger despite receiving clear warnings. The jury awarded the homeowner $173,000 in total property damages. This amount was intended to cover the cost of repairing the structure and other related work needed to fix the damage.Appellate panel rejects appeal and affirms awardThe utility property owner did not accept the jury's decision and filed an appeal with the Appellate Division. The company asked the court to cancel the verdict or order a new trial. It argued that landowners should not automatically be held responsible for natural conditions on their property. It also claimed that the trial judge had made procedural mistakes when explaining a landowner's legal duties to the jury. In its written opinion reviewing docket number A-2181-23, the appeals court rejected these arguments and upheld the full $173,000 award. The appeals judges explained that property owners are generally not responsible for harm caused by purely natural conditions. However, this protection does not apply when an owner knows, or should reasonably know, that a tree in an urban or suburban area is dangerous or badly decayed and fails to take reasonable steps to fix the problem. The court also pointed out that there was strong evidence showing the utility company had received clear warnings about the specific danger posed by the oak tree. The appeals panel found that the trial judge had correctly explained the legal responsibilities of urban property owners to the jury under established New Jersey common law. With the Appellate Division upholding the decision, the trial court's judgment remains in place. The utility property owner must now pay the homeowner $173,000 to cover the losses caused by the fallen tree.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: George Clooney, Don Cheadle and Kerry Washington helped launch a public film school for underserved students; its first class began with 150 pupils
articles.summary: George Clooney, Don Cheadle and Kerry Washington joined forces with entertainment industry leaders to create a public film and television school for
articles.body: George Clooney, Don Cheadle and Kerry Washington joined forces with entertainment industry leaders to create a public film and television school for students from underserved communities in Los Angeles. The Roybal Film and Television Production Magnet opened in August 2022 with an initial class of 150 pupils, offering teenagers an opportunity to explore careers in an industry that has often remained difficult to enter. The initiative aims to make professional training more accessible while helping address the lack of diversity behind the camera in Hollywood.George Clooney and other stars helped establish the public film schoolThe idea behind the Roybal Film and Television Production Magnet grew out of concerns about unequal access to opportunities in the entertainment industry. Although Hollywood has made efforts to improve representation on screen, the people working in production roles behind the camera have not always reflected the diversity of the wider population.According to the Los Angeles Times, Clooney became involved in efforts to create a school that would give young people from less privileged backgrounds a practical route into the film and television business. He worked alongside producing partner Grant Heslov and Creative Artists Agency co-chairman Bryan Lourd to develop the initiative in partnership with the Los Angeles Unified School District.The project was formally established in June 2021, with plans to open the specialised programme the following year. It was set up at the Edward R. Roybal Learning Center in downtown Los Angeles, making film and television education part of an existing public school environment.Clooney was joined by several well-known figures from the entertainment business. Actors Don Cheadle, Kerry Washington, Mindy Kaling and Eva Longoria were among those who supported the project. Their involvement helped bring attention to the school and encouraged major companies to contribute to its development.FOX 11 reported in September 2022 that the academy was designed to create meaningful opportunities for students who might otherwise struggle to access careers in Hollywood.What opportunities does the school offer beyond acting and directingUnlike traditional acting programmes, the Roybal magnet focuses heavily on the jobs that keep film and television productions running. These include camera operators, sound technicians, lighting specialists, make-up artists, set decorators and visual effects professionals.The school was intended to help students gain access to well-paid, often unionised jobs that can be difficult to enter without industry connections. Clooney pointed out that many young people were unaware of the range of careers available behind the camera, despite the demand for skilled workers.FOX 11 reported that the programme was launched at a school where around 90% of students came from families living below the poverty line. The magnet programme incorporates film and television production into classroom learning, allowing pupils to develop practical skills alongside their regular education.Students can also explore careers that do not necessarily require them to become actors, writers or directors. The wider aim is to introduce them to professional opportunities early enough to help them make informed decisions about their futures.How are students getting practical experience in the entertainment industryThe programme goes beyond classroom lessons by giving students opportunities to work on creative projects and learn from people already employed in the entertainment business.LA School Report offered a closer look at how the programme works. Students were learning to develop film concepts, design sets, select costumes and understand how make-up and lighting contribute to storytelling.One assignment involved creating a science-fiction film concept set in 2053. Students Jaison Noralez and Aiyanna Randolph explored how different production elements could help establish the atmosphere of a story.Other projects included producing mock film trailers and creating a horror adaptation of The Wizard of Oz. Pupils learnt how to film and edit their work, use cameras and position microphones to capture dialogue.The school also arranged visits to professional production facilities. Students were given opportunities to visit the Universal Studios Hollywood backlot, tour a local NBC television station and learn about special effects work at KNB EFX, a studio associated with industry professional Howard Berger.The programme also benefits from teachers with professional experience. LA School Report highlighted instructor Brittany Hilgers, who previously worked as a production assistant and screenwriter. Her background allows students to learn about the practical demands of the industry rather than relying solely on theoretical lessons.Kerry Washington, who serves on the school's advisory board, also took part in a question-and-answer session with pupils, giving them an opportunity to interact with someone who has built a career in entertainment.The programme brings Hollywood companies into public educationFinancial support from the entertainment industry has been an important part of getting the school started. According to the Los Angeles Times, the Roybal Film and Television Production Magnet Fund raised more than $4 million for the initiative.Its founding partners included Amazon Studios, Walt Disney, Fox Corporation, NBCUniversal and Telemundo Enterprises, Netflix, Paramount, Sony Pictures Entertainment, the History Channel and A&E Networks, and Warner Bros. Discovery.The programme requires continued financial support to maintain its facilities, training opportunities and industry partnerships. FOX 11 reported in February 2023 that its annual operating costs were approximately $1.5 million.Principal Blanca Cruz explained that partnerships with entertainment companies made it possible to bring real industry experience into the school. The initiative also involves professionals who can introduce students to different areas of production.The Entertainment Industry Foundation, which supports the Roybal programme, describes its broader mission as building a more inclusive group of students prepared for college and careers in film and television.Its programme includes an immersive curriculum for pupils in grades 9 to 12, professional internships, industry knowledge and certifications that can help graduates secure employment.The school hopes to create a lasting route into HollywoodThe Entertainment Industry Foundation estimates that nearly 500 students could benefit from the programme over its first 5 years.The school also plans to strengthen the connection between education and employment. LA School Report noted that students would be matched with industry mentors, with an apprenticeship programme also planned to help them gain experience in their chosen fields.Older pupils can choose specialised areas of study, including post-production, technical work and craft-related careers. An editing studio was also planned to expand the training available to students.The programme has also attracted attention beyond Los Angeles. In February 2023, FOX 11 reported that US Education Secretary Miguel Cardona had visited the school alongside Second Gentleman Doug Emhoff. Cardona described the institution as a model that could be replicated across the country.Clooney had previously expressed hopes that a successful programme could eventually be introduced in other major entertainment centres, including New York, Atlanta and Chicago.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Australian mining heiress and her husband have pledged A$120 million to 10 environmental groups, including A$25 million for Greenpeace, following a multibillion-dollar sale of family iron-ore interests
articles.summary: An Australian mining heiress and her husband have pledged A$120 million to support ten environmental organisations across the country.
articles.body: An Australian mining heiress and her husband have pledged A$120 million to support ten environmental organisations across the country. The donation is one of the largest private contributions to conservation efforts in Australian history. The funding follows a multibillion-dollar sale of family iron-ore interests in Western Australia's Pilbara region. The couple's decision will provide major financial support to local legal, advocacy, and conservation groups working to protect land, oceans, and the climate. Under the funding plan, environmental organisation Greenpeace Australia Pacific will receive the largest single donation. The group has been promised A$25 million to support its long-term campaigns focused on marine protection and climate action.Major grant allocations empower ten conservation groupsThe donation will create a funding programme that provides long-term financial support to ten selected non-profit environmental organisations. According to details reported by The Australian, the total A$120 million package will be shared among ten different groups involved in environmental campaigns, legal work, and conservation. Along with the A$25 million given to Greenpeace Australia Pacific, the remaining money will go to nine other organisations working to restore natural habitats, protect wildlife and biodiversity, and take legal action against environmentally harmful industrial activities. The funding plan is designed to give organisations money that they can use freely for their daily operations. This will allow them to hire more staff, expand their campaigns, and take on longer legal battles without depending entirely on public donations. Representatives of the organisations receiving the money said that large private donations would give them a new opportunity to plan conservation projects over several years. This support is particularly important for protecting Australia's vulnerable regional ecosystems.Wealth origin traces back to Pilbara iron-ore transactionThe money behind this major donation comes from a large financial deal involving family-owned mining interests in the Pilbara region of Western Australia. The family built up significant business interests in iron-ore deposits during the growth of Western Australia's mining industry. A recent multibillion-dollar sale of these family iron-ore rights provided the money needed to make the historic environmental donation. Instead of putting all the proceeds back into other businesses or traditional investments, the heiress and her husband decided to use a large amount of the money to create a dedicated environmental fund. The move represents a notable change in how wealth from the mining industry is being used, with money earned through natural resource extraction now supporting environmental protection and conservation work. Financial commentators and philanthropy experts have highlighted the size of the donation. They noted that private contributions of this scale are still uncommon in Australia's charitable sector. Historically, some of the country's largest donations have gone toward medical research, arts organisations, and universities.Environmental sector reacts to record capital injectionThe announcement of the A$120 million donation has attracted widespread attention across Australia's environmental and non-profit sectors. Greenpeace Australia Pacific welcomed its A$25 million contribution and confirmed that the money would support targeted campaigns to protect marine environments and push for faster reductions in greenhouse gas emissions across major industries. The organisation also noted that having reliable long-term funding would strengthen its independent campaigns across the Pacific and wider Australian territories. Legal advocacy groups receiving part of the remaining funding plan to use the money to protect native habitats, challenge government approvals for projects that produce high levels of emissions, and make sure environmental protection laws are enforced. The distribution of the money will now begin across the ten selected organisations. The donation sets a new example of how private wealth generated through Australia's mining industry can be redirected toward environmental protection, conservation, and long-term care of the country's natural resources.You use AI every day. articles.title: Utah student cited after physical altercation with College Republican caught on camera
articles.summary: Video captures a student appearing to say Republicans "should be shot" before allegedly tackling a College Republican at the University of Utah.
articles.body: A student was cited for simple assault and property damage after allegedly tackling a College Republican at the University of Utah during a confrontation over a campus poll about gender, moments after saying Republicans "should be shot in the streets," according to video of the incident and a university spokesperson. The confrontation unfolded outside the university's Marriott Library, where members of the College Republicans had set up a whiteboard asking whether there are only two genders, The College Fix reported. In a video shared Oct. 28 on X by University of Utah College Republicans officer Rylie Barnes, the student, identified by Fox 13 as Grace, is heard responding to a question about freedom of speech. FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS In the video, a person identified as a College Republican asks the student, "Do you believe we should have the right to freedom of speech?" "No, I think Republicans should be shot in the street, personally," the student replied. The cameraholder says that it sounds like advocacy for violence. After a cut, the video then shows the person identified as a college Republican being knocked to the ground as he yells for the other student to stop; it's unclear how much time transpired between the remarks and the fight. Fox 13 reported, "The student, who identifies herself as Grace, told FOX 13 News that the confrontation was a ‘set up’ and accused College Republicans of instigating and escalating it. She alleges that after she left the table, the Republicans followed her while saying ‘you are denying biology.’ She also says she was punched in the face during the fight." In another interview, she said, "I believe I am a victim of transphobic aggression, and because the University protects the College Republicans and enables them to bully students, I was cited with these bogus charges." CONSERVATIVE JEWISH ACTIVIST VOWS NOT TO BE SILENCED AFTER BEING ATTACKED ON UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN CAMPUS Rebecca Walsh, communications director at the University of Utah, told Fox News Digital in a statement Tuesday, "On Oct. 27 at 12:52 p.m., University of Utah Police responded to reports of a fight between two students on Marriott Plaza." Walsh continued, "While College Republicans were tabling on the plaza, another student approached the table and wiped off a whiteboard with their hand. To the side of the table, that student and one of the students tabling for the College Republicans started to argue about free speech and gender. The visiting student then assaulted the tabling student, knocking them to the ground and tearing their shirt. Police have identified the individual involved and issued two Class B misdemeanor citations--for simple assault and property damage." She added, "The investigation is ongoing. Support and resources have been offered to both students." Walsh also told Fox News Digital that the school could not disclose information about potential student disciplinary proceedings because of federal student privacy laws. Walsh pointed to the university's student code of conduct, which prohibits threats, physical assaults, intimidation and other behavior that endangers the safety of students or members of the campus community, including threats made online. Walsh said the police investigation remains ongoing and the university has offered the alleged victim support and resources through its Student Affairs team. Walsh also emphasized that the university, as a public institution, protects the expression of differing viewpoints, including those of the College Republicans and student groups calling for the citations issued to Grace to be dismissed. Walsh said the university is waiting for the outcome of the police investigation and reiterated that the university condemns threats of violence against anyone on campus and responds swiftly to such incidents. The Utah Anti-War Committee issued a statement supporting who it identified as Amber Grace, writing, "Even though the College Republicans began this harassment, Amber is now facing misdemeanor charges of assault and property damage for resisting transphobia. Amber is a dedicated member of the Salt Lake community as an anti-war activist, and she did nothing wrong by speaking against hateful Republican rhetoric." FOUL-MOUTHED ANTI-WAR PROTESTERS REPEATEDLY DERAIL HEGSETH'S REMARKS AT ARMY EVENT IN DC The Anti-War Committee is calling on Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill to "refuse the charges on Amber Grace! Speaking out against transphobia is not a crime." articles.title: 'Largely true': Trump backs Vance's claim that Iran war cost GOP midterms, says he'd do it again
articles.summary: President Trump supports Vice President Vance's claim that the Iran war impacted the GOP's performance in the 2026 midterm elections, asserting the necessity of military action despite rising fuel prices. Both leaders emphasize the need for a firm stance against Tehran's nuclear ambitions, while examining voter dissatisfaction and potential Democratic challenges.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has acknowledged that the war with Iran contributed to the Republican Party's poor performance in the 2026 midterm elections, citing higher fuel prices as a factor in voter dissatisfaction. However, he defended the military campaign, saying Washington had to act to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Trump agreed with Vice President JD Vance's assessment that the conflict played a role in the party's electoral defeat. He said the rise in petrol prices had affected voters in the short term but maintained that the decision to attack Iran was necessary.Trump said he would take the same course of action again despite the political consequences."Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term, and probably that's uh probably it's true. But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again because long-term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said as cited by ANI.The President also argued that his personal popularity had not translated into votes for Republican candidates. Claiming that his rallies drew large crowds, Trump said the enthusiasm surrounding his appearances had failed to carry over to other members of the party."If I were on the ballot, we would have won. You saw the people, they were packed, thousands and thousands of people were there... But you couldn't just transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies; it was incredible. We weren't able to transfer that love to the candidates," Trump said.Addressing the economic impact of the conflict, Trump identified fuel costs as a key source of voter dissatisfaction. He pointed to the resumption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, saying supplies had increased after being disrupted at the beginning of the conflict."We have tremendous oil flowing out of Hormuz right now. At the beginning, there was none. And probably that's the primary reason, the price, not the war, the price," he said.Trump also said the United States had no alternative but to take military action against Iran, even if it meant facing higher oil prices. He said he had anticipated a larger increase in crude oil costs but considered the operation necessary.The President indicated that he was prepared to work with Democrats following their midterm gains, while warning that he would veto legislation he opposed. He also dismissed the possibility of Democrats pursuing impeachment proceedings, saying such an effort would damage their party."I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that. Because impeachment for no reason. What? For having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in its history," Trump said.Trump made the comments while signing the final steel beam for the White House Ballroom, adding his signature alongside those of workers involved in the construction project.Earlier, Vance had also linked the Republican defeat to the Iran conflict in a lengthy post on X. He rejected claims that the party had lost because of weak voter turnout, arguing that internal polling indicated some people who supported the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 had switched to Democratic candidates in 2026."The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone... The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote.He identified four main concerns among voters who had moved away from the Republicans: ending the war, tackling the cost of living and inflation, maintaining an 'America First' agenda and changing the country's relationship with Israel.Vance also defended calls for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, saying the criticism of the administration's approach reflected concerns among Republican voters. He urged party members to address the reasons behind the defeat rather than blame turnout or other factors.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Andhra, Kerala top ease of vehicle ownership index; UP, Bihar at bottom: Report
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Tamil Nadu have emerged as the top-performing states in ease of vehicle ownership, while Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Tamil Nadu have emerged as the top-performing states in ease of vehicle ownership, while Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal rank at the bottom, reflecting wide disparities in procedures for transferring ownership of used vehicles.The findings are part of the Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index (EVOI) 2026, prepared by Consumer Voice and Indiatech, which assessed systems and procedures across 15 major states and Delhi, covering more than 85% of India’s organised pre-owned vehicle market.None of the states figured in the ‘high ease’ or excellent category, with Andhra Pradesh, the highest-ranked state, scoring only 5.9 on a scale of 0-10. Kerala scored 5.7, followed by Tamil Nadu and Delhi at 4.6 each. Karnataka (4.3), Gujarat (4.2), Madhya Pradesh (4.1), Maharashtra and Telangana (4.1 each) and Punjab (4) occupied the next positions.Rajasthan (4) and Haryana (3.9) were also in the lower half of the rankings, while West Bengal (2.6), Bihar (2.5) and Uttar Pradesh (2.5) brought up the rear.The report comes as India’s pre-owned vehicle market is expanding rapidly and is projected to grow from $36.4 billion in 2025 to over $73.5 billion by 2030. The market has overtaken new vehicle sales in volume. However, fragmented state-level rules, incomplete digitisation and cumbersome procedures continue to impede seamless vehicle ownership transfers.The report, which also included interviews, found that 39% of citizens reported delays in receiving their registration certificates after completing vehicle transfers, while 61.5% were unaware of the requirement for a party-pusher until they reached the respective RTO. articles.title: Chris Mason: The US elections will change Trump – how will Burnham react?
articles.summary: The big question for the British government is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?
articles.body:
The first public words from the prime minister after the American midterm elections were instantly revealing about contemporary international politics and diplomacy.

"Well, President Trump has accepted the results," Andy Burnham said.

It is not an observation British leaders have frequently had to make about recent American presidents – that they are not disputing the result of elections in their own country. But what would previously have been taken for granted no longer can be.

Burnham remains in the foothills of establishing a relationship with the president – so far it has amounted to a handful of phone calls and one face-to-face meeting at the United Nations in New York in September.

As he continues to attempt to build a rapport with Donald Trump, he will be doing so with a president in a wildly different political situation than when Sir Keir Starmer was trying to build bridges with him.

No longer is this a story of an extraordinary comeback, but of a midterm president seemingly punished for the consequences of a foreign war the type of which he had originally promised to avoid.

Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results

Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad

And it is noticeable that the British government's public reaction is grounded too in the consequences of the war with Iran: the cost of living.

"I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all and that's the cost of living," the prime minister said.

"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict between in Ukraine started by Russia."

Within government the Iran war and its consequences, particularly on energy prices, is widely seen as the biggest individual contributor among the many factors currently driving up the cost of living.

And, bluntly, it is one that puts many, including many of America's allies, in alignment with many in America, Democrat and Republican, who when asked why these elections went as they did, point at the prices displayed outside any petrol station.

Speaking before the votes in America were counted, the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband reflected on this when I spoke to him on BBC Newscast .

When I asked him specifically if he feared that a domestically humiliated Trump may prove more belligerent internationally, it was to the Iran war the foreign secretary referred.

He didn't offer a direct answer to my question, but chose instead to say this: "I know that one of the biggest responsibilities of the whole government, frankly, is the cost of living situation at home, and we know one of the biggest contributors to the cost of living situation is, frankly, the conflict."

"The Strait of Hormuz being not exactly closed, but not properly open, not free flowing, and that is hitting families at home," he said.

"We know that we need a diplomatic way out of this conflict, and so that is one of the things that we're working on. It's something I talked to the U.S. Secretary of State about at the G20, and it's something we continue to work on," he added.

The foreign secretary met Marco Rubio at the meeting in Atlanta last week.

But the big question for the British government, and so many others, is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?

Or, do America's traditional allies, the UK, the European Union, Canada, Australia and others feel more strident and willing to work with Donald Trump's domestic political opponents to try to challenge and restrain a weakened president?

The answers to these two final questions will determine much in world affairs in the next couple of years.

articles.title: Whoopi Goldberg warns Democrats to 'take care of business' after midterm wins
articles.summary: Whoopi Goldberg delivered a blunt warning to Democrats on "The View" after their midterm sweep, demanding they focus on taking care of business and avoid infighting.
articles.body: "The View" co-host Whoopi Goldberg warned Democrats on Wednesday after they regained control of both chambers of Congress that they need to "take care of business." "A note to the Democrats, we put you in to take care of business. We don’t want to know what your back-biting fighting is, we don’t want to hear it. You can kvetch at each other after you take care of the people’s business," Goldberg said. Democrats recaptured majorities in the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, riding a massive blue wave that will give them control of both chambers in January 2027. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE The co-hosts also interviewed Democratic Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico during the show, after he flipped a Republican-held U.S. Senate seat. Talarico told the co-hosts that he wanted to work with President Donald Trump to provide some "affordability crisis relief" to Texans, suggesting a suspension of federal gasoline and diesel taxes. "I want to work with both parties, I want to work with President Trump to try to provide some relief to working Texans in the middle of this affordability crisis," he said. "I think we could suspend the federal gas tax and the federal diesel tax. That would provide some immediate relief at the pump for working families. Everybody, when you fill up your tank, you are paying a hidden tax, and this federal gas tax, if we suspend it, it could drop the price of gas by 18 cents a gallon immediately." "And I know that’s not everything, we’re not going to be able to get the prices lower until we end this disastrous war in Iran, but it could provide necessary relief in the short term for the hard-working families in our state," Talarico added. TRUMP'S GAMBLE ON KEN PAXTON BACKFIRES AS DEMOCRAT PULLS OFF HISTORIC TEXAS SENATE UPSET At the end of the interview, Goldberg told Talarico, "Senator-elect, congratulations, man. We were thrilled with your win, you are where you should be." "Whoopi let her excitement get the better of her. It’s another instance of ABC’s purported ‘bona fide news program’ boldly saying the quiet part out loud and admitting that the show is 100 percent meant to be [a] vector to push Democratic Party propaganda to the American people to influence elections," the Media Research Center's NewsBusters associate editor Nicholas Fondacaro told Fox News Digital in a statement. "In the months and weeks leading up to the midterms, 'The View' was actively telling people to not only vote for Democrats but also vote for specific candidates like James Talarico. The use of the public broadcast spectrum to electioneer for a party or candidate by a licensee is a violation of federal regulations," he continued. "The View and ABC were already under intense scrutiny from the FCC before Whoopi’s comments and they’re likely to be used against the network in any potential action by the commission." ABC did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Talarico also expressed a willingness to work with Trump during an interview on "The Diary of a CEO" podcast, released Monday. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEMOCRATS FACE AN IMPEACHMENT TRACTOR BEAM THAT COULD DERAIL THEIR AFFORDABILITY MESSAGE "I would love, as the next U.S. senator from Texas, to work with Donald Trump to actually fulfill some of the promise of his political project," Talarico told host Steven Bartlett. "The promise of MAGA was that we were going to transform this government so that it delivered for the people who have been left behind, the people who have been forgotten in this country. And there's still time to do that," Talarico continued. The co-hosts of "The View" agreed with comments from former Vice President Kamala Harris during a podcast appearance last month, saying that Democrats should not pursue impeachment proceedings against Trump if they won control of Congress. "In terms of Trump, no, I don't think that's what should be on the agenda," co-host Sunny Hostin said. "Hakeem Jeffries — who I believe will be the next speaker of the House, after November — he has a plan for 100 days, which includes tax credits, taking care of the tax credits, limiting ICE and also stock trades." "And then he's got a plan for the first 100 hours, which would include, you know, just undoing a lot of unpopular Trump policies. So, I think there is a plan in place that Democrats have, and it may not include impeaching Trump," she added. articles.title: Canadian mother and daughter dead after suspected grizzly bear attack on hiking trail
articles.summary: Jennifer Balcarras and Selah Reed went missing on a hiking trail minutes from their Bella Coola home before a suspected grizzly bear attack.
articles.body: A Canadian woman and her daughter were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack over the weekend while hiking on a trail near their home, according to authorities. Jennifer Balcarras, 48, an art therapist, and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, went missing Saturday after going for a walk on the Snooka West Trail, just minutes from their home in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Loved ones grew concerned when Balcarras failed to show up for a scheduled online meet-up on Saturday, her brother, Matt Balcarras, told The Vancouver Sun. A PRACTICAL GUIDE TO NOT GETTING MAULED BY A BEAR WHILE HIKING OR CAMPING THIS SUMMER After failing to reach the pair, relatives asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) for a welfare check on Sunday morning. Authorities discovered Balcarras' vehicle parked at the trailhead. Her body was recovered Monday, and search teams found Reed's body on Tuesday. GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL "There was evidence to suggest a bear may have been involved," Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service, said in a video update posted to social media. Tyre noted that officers were actively working to "locate and capture any bears involved" and said it was not immediately clear if more than one animal was responsible. HIDDEN DANGER AT POPULAR US NATIONAL PARK FORCES TRAIL CLOSURES AS BEAR SIGHTINGS CLIMB "Any captured bear will be assessed," conservation officials added in a statement. "If it is determined to have been involved in the attack, it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety." Matt Balcarras expressed shock over the location of the attack, emphasizing that his sister and niece were experienced in the region. "They were not naive city folks," he said. "They were strong women living the life." articles.summary: In a result that would have seemed fanciful even a few months ago, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican governor Greg Abbott, becoming
articles.body: In a result that would have seemed fanciful even a few months ago, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican governor Greg Abbott, becoming the first Latina governor of a state that was successively a province of Spanish America, a Mexican territory, and an independent sovereign republic before being annexed into the United States.Texas also elected Democrat James Talarico to the Senate, the first Democratic senator from the state since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.Similar political convulsions in Maine saw Democrat Troy Jackson defeat Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine, ending her nearly 30-year Senate career that was considered impregnable.South Carolina, a Republican bastion, elected Democrat Annie Andrews to the Senate, defeating Darlene Graham, sister of four-term senator Lindsay Graham. Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, delivered another stunning upset, sending Adam Hamilton to Washington. Democrats also captured Senate seats in Michigan (Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator in US history), Ohio (Sherrod Brown), Iowa (Josh Turek) and New Hampshire, where Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man to be elected to the Senate.The results were less a blue wave than a political tsunami, sweeping away some of the GOP's most deeply entrenched assumptions that pre-date Trump, who effectively took the party down with him because the shock extended well beyond the Senate. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in American history, while Ohio went to Democrat Amy Acton who defeated Indian-American Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy. Candidates behind whom Trump put his heart, soul, and body, often telling voters to assume he was on the ballot, were sent packing.The rout shocked and angered even conservatives, many of whom began to turn on Trump. "It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told BBC, calling it "a disaster of the first magnitude" that nobody saw coming.Actually, every poll and survey other than MAGA-affiliated ones saw it coming, although the scale was not foreseen by most. In fact, Democrats went to polling day wary of the "too good to be true" projections given past setbacks, particularly in 2016 when Trump himself did not appear to believe he would win. This time around, he tried to conjure up victory in the face of imminent defeat, but voters had other ideas.Convulsions were afoot even within the Democratic Party, with radicals and progressives making a mark, most notably in Los Angeles where Democrat Socialist Nithya Raman was leading establishment Democrat Karen Bass by a narrow 16,000 votes in the mayoral election as the time of writing.
